To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
a genetic factor in the Copenhagen rat is inherited in a dominant fashion and is expressed in the mammary glands themselves.

(1) a gene from the resistant Copenhagen rat (COP) can suppress the highly susceptible response of the female mammary gland of five different inbred rat strains to DMBA exposure; and (2) this suppression is not due to host systemic factors but to a genetic factor within the donor mammary glands themselves.

the genetic factor(s) responsible for the resistance of the COP female rat to DMBA-induced adenocarcinoma of the mammary gland is (are) active in suppressing the high susceptibility to DMBA-induced breast cancer in F1 hybrids produced from cross-breeding COP to the highly susceptible strains.

The main takeaway from our work is that
the mammary gland is a complex organ and that the genetic makeup of this organ determines its response to carcinogenic insult.
the genetic makeup of a mammary gland can determine its response to a chemical carcinogen and that this response is not dependent on host systemic factors.
the COP gene which confers resistance to DMBA-induced carcinogenesis is a genetic factor in the mammary tissue itself and not in the host systemic level.
